passages.original: — Tum mater: Si bona, inquit, uelit et habeat, beatus est, si autem mala uelit, quamuis habeat. miser est. ■— (\'Cui ego arridens atque gestiens: Ipsam, inquam, prorsus, mater, arcem philosophiae tenuisti. nam tibi procul dubio uerba defuerunt, ut non sicut Tullius te modo panderes, cuius de hac sententia uerba ista sunt. nam in Hortensio. quem de laude ac defensione philosophiae librum fecit: ecce autem. ait, non philosophi quidem, sed promti tamen ad disputandum omnes aiunt esse beatos, qui uiuant ut ipsi uelint.
passages.english: Then my mother said: "If he wants good things and has them, he is happy; but if he wants bad things, even though he has them, he is wretched." Smiling at her and delighted, I said: "Mother, you have plainly taken the very citadel of philosophy. For no doubt you lacked only the words to express yourself just now as Tully [Cicero] did, whose words on this view are these. For in the Hortensius, the book he wrote in praise and defence of philosophy, he says: 'But look: not philosophers indeed, but people ready for argument, all say that those are happy who live as they themselves wish.'"
passages.notes: Scanning debris at the start of Monica's reply and of Augustine's response ("■—", "(\'Cui") has been ignored, and "miser est" is read in place of the stray full stop after "habeat". The quotation from Cicero's Hortensius continues in the following passage.

passages.original: Quod cum placuit omnibus: Bene habet, inquam, sed adhuc illud uereor, ne uos moueat quod iam superius concesseramus, miserum esse quisquis beatus non esset; cui consequens erit esse miserum hominem, qui ∗∗∗∗∗∗ aliquem beatum. an uero, quod ait Tullius, multorum interrispraediorumdominos diuites appellamus, omnium uirtutum poss\'essores pauperes nominabimus? sed illud uidete, utrum, quomodo uerum est, quod omnis egens miser sit, ita sit uerum, quod omnis miser egeat.
passages.english: When this pleased everyone, I said: "Good. But I am still afraid that you may be troubled by what we conceded earlier, that whoever was not happy was wretched. From this it will follow that a man is wretched who [...] someone happy. Or indeed, as Tully says, shall we call the owners of many estates on earth rich, and name the possessors of all the virtues poor? But consider this: just as it is true that everyone in want is wretched, whether it is likewise true that everyone wretched is in want."
passages.notes: The edition marks a lacuna (asterisks) in the clause beginning "cui consequens erit esse miserum hominem, qui"; its sense cannot be recovered. "interrispraediorumdominos" is read as "in terris praediorum dominos".

passages.original: nam huic sententiae concedendae difficultatem illa res facit, quod multis in magna fortuitarum rerum copia constitutis, quibus ita facilia sunt omnia, ut ad eorum nutum praesto sit quidquid cupiditas poscit, difficilis quidem ista uita est. sed fingamus aliquem tamen, qualem Tullius fuisse dicit Oratam. quis enim facile dicat Oratam egestate laborasse, hominem ditissimum amoenissimum deliciosis simun, cui neque ad uoluptatem quicquam defuit neque ad gratiam neque ad bonam integramque ualetudinem ?
passages.english: For the difficulty in conceding this view comes from the fact that, for many who are placed amid a great abundance of things that depend on fortune, and for whom everything is so easy that whatever desire demands is ready at their nod, this life is indeed hard. But let us nevertheless imagine someone such as Tully says Orata was. For who would readily say that Orata suffered from want, a very rich man, a very charming one, a most luxurious one, who lacked nothing for pleasure, nor for favour, nor for good and sound health?
passages.notes: "difficilis quidem ista uita est" is puzzling here; the sense may be that such a life is hard to call wretched, or the text may be corrupt. "deliciosis simun" is read as "deliciosissimum".

passages.original: at etiam hic similiter, ut in nequitia et frugalitate, apparent illa duo, esse et non esse, et, si egestas est ipsa stultitia, plenitudo erit sapientia. merito etiam uirtutum omnium matrem multi frugalitatem esse dixerunt. quibus consentiens Tullius etiam in populari oratione ait: ut uolet quisque accipiat; ego tamen frugalitatem, id\' est modestiam et temperantiam, uirtutem maximam iudico : prorsus doctissime ac decentissime; considerauit enim frugem, id est illud, quod esse dicimus, cui est non esse contrarium. sed propter uulgarem loquendi consuetudinem, qua frugalitas quasi parsimonia dici solet, duobus consequentibus quid senserit inlustrauit subiciendo modestiam et temperantiam;
passages.english: But here too, just as with worthlessness and frugality, those two things appear, being and not-being; and if want is folly itself, fullness will be wisdom. Rightly too have many said that frugality is the mother of all the virtues. Agreeing with them, Tully says even in a popular speech: "Let each take it as he wishes; I, however, judge frugality, that is, moderation and temperance, to be the greatest virtue." [This was said] most learnedly and most fittingly; for he had in mind *frux* [fruit, worth], that is, that which we say *is*, to which not-being is opposed. But because of the common usage of speech, in which frugality is usually spoken of as if it were thrift, he made clear what he meant by adding two consequent terms, moderation and temperance;
passages.notes: The argument rests on the etymological link between Latin frugalitas and frux/frugem, which cannot be reproduced in English. Augustine treats frugem as standing for 'being'. The Cicero quotation is from a speech (Pro Deiotaro).
